title: Fever Pitch
full_review:
A budding Boston romance gets thrown a comic curveball in the sweet and funny romantic comedy �Fever Pitch� (20th Century Fox), a tale about love, laughter and baseball.

Unfortunately, as with most contemporary love stories, the courtship in �Fever Pitch� involves a premarital living arrangement, precluding an unqualified thumbs-up. But apart from that, directors Bob and Peter Farrelly have hit a home run.

Drew Barrymore stars as Lindsey Meeks, a 30-year-old workaholic business consultant whose competitive drive and professional ambition have put her social life on hold.

Jimmy Fallon co-stars as Ben Wrightman, a goofy but charming high school math teacher who meets Lindsey during a class outing to the office where she works.

Though she seems out of his league, they immediately hit it off. After a few months of dating, Lindsey tells her friends that Ben may be Mr. Right.

But Ben is hiding a dark secret: He is a rabid Red Sox fan. He inherited his all-consuming passion for the perennial also-rans � along with his much-coveted season tickets � from his Uncle Carl (Lenny Clarke) when he was just a boy. (Ben�s apartment is a veritable shrine to the team complete with a wall painted like Fenway Park�s legendary �Green Monster� scoreboard.)

At first, Lindsey admires his fervor: �You have a lyrical soul, you can love under the best and worst conditions.� That is, until opening day rolls around and �normal� Ben gives way to �crazy� Ben, who for six months each year obsessively organizes his existence around the team�s schedule. He even passes up a relationship-saving trip to Paris with Lindsey rather than jeopardize his perfect game attendance.

What unfolds is a love triangle: a boy, a girl and a baseball team.

Without giving anything away, let�s just say that this is that rarest of sports subgenres: a Red Sox movie with a happy ending.

Barrymore is at the top of her game, bringing to the screen her usual blend of effervescent girl-next-door charm and comic dexterity. Fallon, after striking out in �Taxi,� is quite good here as the likeable man-child.

Filmed in and around Boston (with Toronto standing in for some shots), the movie has an authentic feel, helped greatly by actual game footage and by Fenway Park location shooting � including the big romantic climax.

Set against the improbable 2004 baseball season, when the boys from Beantown made history by ending their 86-year drought and winning the World Series, �Fever Pitch� has a storybook magic about it.

Loosely based on a novel by British author Nick Hornby (with baseball replacing soccer in the Americanized movie), �Fever Pitch� imparts an admirable message about how love demands both acceptance and sacrifice.

Of course, viewers may take offense at the film�s unnecessary sexual intimations, as well as an off-screen scene involving unneeded, stomach-churning vomit sound effects.

Hopeless romantics and baseball enthusiasts will undoubtedly be entertained, but even those who think a �stolen base� is a felony will find themselves cheering by the end, New York Yankees fans excepted. Only don�t expect a sequel for another 86 years.

The film contains implied premarital sex, some comic violence and crude humor, as well as scattered crass expressions. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III � adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 � parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
